title: Rewrite the notes until they settle
allegory: Policy evaluation is like a board game where every square keeps a sticky note saying 'what I will collect from here if I follow the plan': each round every note is rewritten from the notes one step ahead, so news of each prize spreads outward a square per round, shrinking a little each step, until no note changes.
map: a sticky note on each square: what I will collect from here
the plan pinned to each square
rewrite: this step's prize plus a shrunk copy of the note where you land
the Bellman update V(s) ← Σ T(s'|s,π(s))·[R + γV(s')]
news of a prize spreading one square per round, shrinking by γ
each sweep propagates value one more step back, discounted
stop when no note moves by more than a hair
stop when max |V_new − V_old| < eps: the fixed point V_π

chapters.name: Is this plan good?
chapters.note: from every square: which way to step. but how good is that?

cap.1: You have a plan: from each square of a little world, which way to step. Before changing it, you need to know how good it is from every square.
cap.2: A policy fixes one action per state. Its value V(s) is the expected discounted reward from s onwards, averaged over the random slips in where each move lands.
cap.3: Given π and a known model T(s,a,s'), R(s,a,s'), compute V_π(s) = E[Σ γᵗ rₜ | s₀ = s, π]. Policy evaluation is the prediction half of policy iteration.

cap.1: Give each square a sticky note: 'what I'll collect from here'. Each round, rewrite it as this step's prize plus a shrunk copy of the note where you land.
cap.2: Start every note at 0. One sweep rewrites all squares from the old notes. A prize's news spreads one square further per sweep, shrinking by γ each step: 1, 0.9, 0.81.
cap.3: Iterative evaluation applies the Bellman expectation operator to an arbitrary V₀. With γ = 0.9 and deterministic moves, value decays geometrically with distance to the reward.

cap.1: New note = the average, over where your step might land, of (prize for this step + γ × the note there). γ, a bit under 1, shrinks faraway prizes.
cap.2: policy_eval_numerical: repeat this for all states until max |V_new - V_old| < eps. T and R arrive as arrays: env.T[s, a, s'], env.R[s, a, s'].
cap.3: V ← r^π + γP^πV. For γ < 1 this operator is a γ-contraction in the sup norm, so the iterates converge geometrically to its unique fixed point, V_π.

cap.1: Each round, the notes get closer to their true values by at least a factor of γ. With γ = 0.9 the error shrinks fast; with 0.99 it takes many more rounds.
cap.2: The worst-case error after k sweeps is at most γᵏ times the starting error. Far-sighted agents, γ near 1, need many more sweeps to settle.
cap.3: ‖V_k − V_π‖∞ ≤ γᵏ‖V₀ − V_π‖∞. To shrink the bound a thousandfold takes about 66 sweeps at γ = 0.9 and about 690 at γ = 0.99.

chapters.name: Solve it once
chapters.verdict: With the plan fixed, the notes are just simultaneous equations.

cap.1: With the plan fixed, all the notes' rules together are ordinary simultaneous equations, so you can solve them in one go. Both ways give the same numbers.
cap.2: Howard (1960): v = (I − γP^π)⁻¹ r^π. ARENA has you write both and check they agree on the same gridworld before trusting either.
cap.3: (I − γP)⁻¹ = Σ γᵏPᵏ, the discounted sum over every horizon; each sweep from V₀ = 0 adds one more term. The exact solve is cubic in states, fine for small tabular worlds.

cap.1: Set γ to exactly 1 and far prizes stop shrinking. In a world where you can wander forever, the notes can keep growing and never settle.
cap.2: With γ = 1 the update is no longer a contraction: policy_eval_numerical can creep upward forever, and I - γP can be singular, so the exact solve fails too.
cap.3: γ < 1 keeps the spectral radius of γP^π below 1, giving both invertibility and convergence. Keep γ < 1 in the tabular exercises and assert the two evaluators agree within eps.

cap.1: Scoring a fixed plan is half of getting better: score it, change the choices that scored badly, repeat. Every later RL method does a version of this.
cap.2: SARSA, Q-learning and DQN run this loop with the map taken away: sampled transitions instead of T and R arrays. The critic in actor-critic methods is a learned policy evaluator.
cap.3: Value estimation underlies the critics used to RL-train language models, such as PPO's value head in RLHF, so knowing what a value means is part of understanding and steering trained behaviour.

coda.title: A 30-square corridor with a prize at the left end

readouts.label: worst error left on the corridor

caption.1: Add sweeps and watch news of the prize spread one square per sweep. Raise γ and far squares care more about the prize, so there is more left to learn.
caption.2: After k sweeps from zero, only squares within k steps know about the prize. The worst error left is γᵏ: the contraction at work, slow when γ is near 1.
caption.3: From V₀ = 0, V_k is the Neumann series truncated after k terms. On this deterministic corridor the sup-norm error is exactly γᵏ until news reaches the far end.

where_else: Q-learning and DQN: the same Bellman backup, with samples instead of the full map
The critic in actor-critic and PPO: a network trained to do policy evaluation
PageRank and heat diffusion: values that settle by repeatedly averaging their neighbours

hamming.what: Working out how much reward a fixed plan collects from each state, by applying the Bellman equation repeatedly until the numbers stop changing.
hamming.when: Before improving a policy, and inside every RL method that learns a value function or a critic.
hamming.why: You cannot improve a plan you cannot score, and the Bellman rewrite turns 'sum over all futures' into a local rule that provably settles.

object.title: The value staircase
object.subtitle: A 7 by 7 board whose squares rise towards the prize corner, built one step per sweep.

cap.1: Every note starts at 0: a flat board, with the prize waiting in one corner.
cap.2: V₀ = 0 everywhere. The plan walks straight towards the prize corner.
cap.3: Arbitrary initialisation; the contraction pulls any starting V towards V_π.

cap.1: After 3 rounds, news of the prize has reached only the squares within 3 steps of it.
cap.2: Each sweep propagates value one more step back: a staircase grows out from the prize.
cap.3: V_k equals V_π on states within k steps of the reward and is still 0 beyond.

cap.1: After enough rounds every square knows: a staircase that drops by a factor γ with each step away.
cap.2: The fixed point: V(s) = γ^distance for this deterministic plan towards the prize.
cap.3: V_π for a deterministic shortest-path policy with a single terminal reward is γᵈ.

cap.1: With a short-sighted γ = 0.5 the staircase is steep: faraway squares barely care about the prize.
cap.2: Small γ discounts the future heavily, so values fall fast with distance.
cap.3: The effective horizon is roughly 1/(1 − γ): about 2 steps at γ = 0.5, about 100 at γ = 0.99.

cap.1: With γ = 0.99 the staircase is nearly flat: every square values the prize almost fully.
cap.2: Large γ makes values far-sighted; in worlds with loops and slips it also means many more sweeps to settle.
cap.3: The contraction factor is γ, so worst-case sweeps to a tolerance ε scale like log(1/ε)/(1 − γ).

predict.q: After 4 sweeps from all-zero notes, which squares know about the prize?

options.t: Only those within 4 steps of it

predict.why: Each sweep copies news one step further back. Squares further away still read 0.

predict.q: You set γ = 1 in a world where the agent can wander forever. What happens?

options.t: The notes may never settle, and the exact solve can fail

predict.why: Without discounting the update is no longer a contraction, and I − γP can be singular.

object.where: Anything that settles by repeatedly averaging neighbours: heat spreading across a plate, PageRank, gossip reaching everyone.
